headline: The U.S. Army’s AH-64 'Apache' fleet is experiencing an unusually high rate of serious accidents, with five Class A mishaps so far in FY2026. A CNN analysis puts the current rate at roughly 6.24 Class A crashes per 100,000 flight hours, approaching the Army’s recent worst year of 2024, when the fleet recorded nine major crashes at a rate of 7.02 per 100,000 hours. The spike comes amid a separate, unresolved transmission problem affecting roughly 10% of the Army’s Apache fleet. Army safety messages identified 70 potentially faulty transmissions in April and another 10 in July. Failures can potentially affect the tail rotor, electrical power and hydraulics, creating the possibility of a sudden loss of control. The Army has not said how many of this year’s crashes are attributable to the transmission issue, and specifically cautions that its inclusion in safety reviews does not establish causation for any individual mishap. The root cause of the transmission failures remains under investigation, with Boeing assisting Army maintenance personnel. The latest fatal crash occurred Aug. 12 near Fort Hood, Texas, killing two pilots and prompting a temporary Army-wide pause in Apache training flights. That stand-down ended Wednesday, although deployed units in the Middle East were exempt. Source: https://edition.cnn.com/2026/08/24/politics/us-army-attack-helicopters-crashing-at-historically-high-rate

headline: Nearly six months after the Navy evacuated about 1,300 family members from Bahrain, the service is telling them they should not expect to return anytime soon according to reporting from Stars & Stripes. The prolonged evacuation has exposed major gaps in the military's relocation system. Families report tens of thousands of dollars in unreimbursed expenses, stranded vehicles and household goods, repeated moves, and uncertainty over housing, schools and medical care. Vice Adm. Curt Renshaw, commander of U.S. Naval Forces Central Command, acknowledged the problem directly, telling evacuees: “We literally have been making this up as we go, because nothing is conceived to go on this length of time.” The Navy is now directing dependents to designate a new permanent duty station, generally in the U.S, where their belongings can be delivered and they can transition out of temporary safe haven status. They could potentially return if conditions improve. Source: https://www.stripes.com/branches/navy/2026-08-21/bahrain-evacuation-military-families-navy-22618186.html

headline: The U.S. Navy has publicly disclosed a previously unannounced AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missile (LRAAM), also known as the "Malice", revealing the weapon mounted inside the internal weapons bay of an F-35C Lightning II with an AIM-120 AMRAAM mounted on the bay door. The Navy describes the AIM-424 as its next-generation, long range air to air missile, intended to give Navy and Marine Corps aviators greater capability against advanced threats. The internal carriage is particularly significant. Rather than simply adding another externally carried long-range missile, the AIM-424 appears to have been designed around the F-35's limited internal weapons-bay dimensions, allowing the aircraft to retain its low-observable configuration while carrying a substantially longer-range air-to-air weapon. The missile is still associated with testing and development, and the Navy has released few technical details regarding its range, seeker, propulsion or intended employment. The available imagery does, however, show the AIM-424 being evaluated on both the F-35C and F/A-18E/F, indicating that the weapon is being considered across the Navy's carrier aviation force. Source: https://www.dvidshub.net/image/9879420/aim-424-long-range-air-air-missile-lraam

headline: The USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) has left the Middle East after 274 days deployed, with the carrier strike group now operating in the Indian Ocean under U.S. 7th Fleet, according to USNI. The carrier departed San Diego on Nov. 25 and has been at sea since its last port visit in Guam on Dec. 11—more than eight months without a port call, breaking the previous 206-day record set by USS Dwight D. Eisenhower during the COVID-19 pandemic. The unusually long deployment was compounded by the loss of regional logistics hubs following Iranian attacks, forcing Navy supply ships to travel thousands of miles to sustain the carrier and other forces operating in the Arabian Sea. The Navy says resupply problems improved after new supply lines were established. Lincoln is being replaced in the region by the forward deployed USS George Washington (CVN-73), which arrived two days ago and will join USS George H.W. Bush (CVN-77) to maintain a two carrier presence amid the war with Iran. From the Western Indian Ocean, it will take Lincoln 3-4 weeks to transit across the Pacific back to San Diego. An open question is whether the ship will make a port call on the way home, which would extend the deployment a few days. The Navy is now dealing with a broader pattern of extended deployments: USNI notes that carrier deployments since October 2023 have averaged about 8½ months, while USS Gerald R. Ford recently completed a record 326-day deployment. Source: https://news.usni.org/2026/08/22/uss-abraham-lincoln-leaves-the-middle-east-after-almost-7-months

headline: The Pentagon is moving to dismiss the publisher, editor-in-chief and a reporter at Stars and Stripes, citing insubordination. The notices reportedly stem from interviews in which Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin and reporter Lara Korte defended the publication’s editorial independence and said Pentagon interference in news coverage would cross a red line. The move comes after Stars and Stripes reported on difficult conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, including concerns about sailors’ mental health during its extended deployment—reports that Pentagon leadership and President Trump disputed. Publisher Max Lederer, who has led the paper for 19 years, had already announced plans to retire in September, citing fundamental differences with the administration over the publication’s mission. Source: https://www.cbsnews.com/news/stars-and-stripes-publisher-editor-separation-notices-pentagon/

headline: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Iran. Key points: • The U.S. Treasury has begun Operation Economic Outcast, an unprecedented campaign against the Islamic Republic. The objective: sever every economic lifeline that sustains the regime until Tehran stands alone. • "Under Trump, America is no longer managing the Iranian threat. We are ending it." • Iran has two paths: complete global isolation or a path back to normalcy. • A zero-leakage approach to block every potential source of revenue that funds the IRGC and the regime. • Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the U.S. dollar system. • On China: "No one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions." Anyone facilitating transactions in the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, will be targeted. • Trump is making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime. • "It is now time for world leaders to make the decision between America and Iran." • A major financial institution expected to be sanctioned by end of week. • "I am not going to set timelines, but we do not have infinite patience here." • Iran's currency crashed through 2 million rials to the dollar. Central Bank Governor Hemmati admitted the simultaneous drop in oil revenues, tax income, and social security contributions "has affected every part of Iran's economy."
